title: Potential for sustainable use of trees in hot arid regions: a case study of Emirati neighborhoods in Abu Dhabi
abstract: This paper explores the future of landscapes in arid, coastal regions based on 4 water-energy regimes, using a case study of villa neighborhoods in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates. It examines the potential for the planting of 15 selected tree species for carbon storage under various water-energy regimes to create carbon neutral (or negative) villa neighborhoods. Recent improvements to solar photovoltaic and reverse-osmosis desalination technology have lowered the carbon emissions for water production by over 99% relative to current gas-powered multi-stage flash desalination (0.08 kg CO2/m3 vs.12.8 kg CO2/m3). This allows trees planted in hot, desert climates to utilize treated ocean water while net sequestering between 1.7 and 38.2 kg C/tree/yr depending on species. When planted in existing neighborhood open spaces, we find that net carbon storage rates from trees are significant (15–800%) relative to operational emissions rates for building energy (cooling, lighting, equipment) when households are supplied from 100% renewable energy sources. Thus, as technology advances, landscape design strategies in the region could evolve to maximize planting to sequester carbon while also creating more comfortable outdoor spaces that enhance the livability of neighborhoods. This study provides a first step in identifying the potential for landscape architectural design to employ a tree-based, neighborhood scale, carbon storage strategy in arid regions such as those in the Arabian Peninsula. As nations move towards a carbon-neutral future, it is imperative to develop innovative solutions that address urban sustainability, especially in resource-challenged and extreme climate regions where new urban development is planned.

## **1. Introduction**

Demographic growth and climate change are projected to have significant impacts on the availability and quality of water resources globally. With growing urbanization, desert (hyper-arid) regions, which occupy approximately 11 percent of the total global land area, are projected to expand and to witness increased aridity (Gamo, Shinoda, & Maeda, 2013; Sowers, Vengosh, & Weinthal, 2011). These regions are characterized by sparse vegetation due to high aridity and have acutely limited access to freshwater resources (Forest Management Division, Forestry Department, 1989).

With escalating pressure on already insufficient water resources, cities in coastal arid regions are increasingly relying on desalination to provide water for urban uses. Globally, more than 300 million people rely on desalinated water for some or all of their daily needs, and over 86 million cubic meters of water is desalinated per day (International Desalination Association, n.d.; Voutchkov, 2016). Forty-four percent of this capacity is located in the Middle East and North Africa (MENA) – a region characterized by hyper-aridity and low vegetation (Sowers et al., 2011; Voutchkov, 2016). In this region, the prominent technology used for desalination is multi-stage thermal co-generation, where energy and desalinated water are co-produced. These plants are energy and capital intensive (Yu, Deshazo, Stenstrom, & Cohen, 2015), and produce multiple environmental externalities, such as carbon emissions and highsalinity discharge (Assaf & Nour, 2014; Miller, Shemer, & Semiat, 2015). The region also faces the threat of deteriorating water quality, more prolonged droughts, and more variable rainfall events (Sowers et al., 2011).

In many parts of the MENA region, especially in the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) nations, a combination of desalinated water, reused wastewater, and groundwater is used for the ‘greening’ of urban desert landscapes (Sowers et al., 2011). For example, in the United Arab Emirates (UAE) approximately 83 percent of the total water demand is from the green sector which includes the irrigation of street trees and parks (Shahin & Salem, 2014a, 2014b).

These nations also have some of the highest per capita carbon footprints in the world and are actively working towards reducing their emissions (World Wildlife Fund, 2016). In an attempt to provide sustainable development solutions for arid regions globally, we use the case study of Emirati residential neighborhoods in Abu Dhabi, UAE, to explore the future of landscaping within the framework of existing climatic and geographic limitations. We use future technology adoption scenarios to estimate the environmental impacts of neighborhood scale afforestation under various water-energy nexuses. We ask: In regions where hyper-aridity creates the need for desalination of water for even basic human needs, can technology and design create synergies to make suburban landscapes carbon neutral (or carbon negative)? What is the magnitude of calculated neighborhood scale carbon storage relative to household emissions?

## _1.1. Sustainability and villa neighborhoods in the GCC and Abu Dhabi_

In Abu Dhabi, the capital of the UAE, 55 percent of the urban landscape consists of villa (detached single-family house) neighborhoods (as per initial GIS calculations) (Fig. 1). A majority of these neighborhoods are home to local Emiratis who form only 19 percent of the total population of 2.78 million (Abu Dhabi Digital Government, 2018). Here, a typical neighborhood consists of arterial and sub-arterial streets lined with residential plots. A central space is allotted for a community mosque, small retail, and public open space. Streets are often planted with date palm trees. Plots are allotted to Emirati families through a welfare program administered by the Abu Dhabi Housing Authority (ADHA). The open space between the villa and the plot boundary walls is either left bare (Fig. 1), or vegetated with lush and water-intensive turfgrass and date palm trees (Remali, Salama, Wiedmann, & Ibrahim, 2016). The former results in increased UHI

(Lazzarini, Marpu, & Ghedira, 2013), while the latter results in either high net negative storage when watered from multi-stage flash desalination sources, or the depletion of limited recycled water sources. Scholars have criticized villa neighborhoods, therefore, for their high resource consumption rates and negative environmental impact (Jabareen, 2006). This paper focuses primarily on the impact of changes to the water-energy nexus in Abu Dhabi based on environmentally appropriate landscaping at the neighborhood scale.

## _1.2. Current landscaping trends in Abu Dhabi_

In addition to high household resource consumption rates, open spaces also contribute to the unsustainable use of land in villa neighborhoods. Interstitial spaces are often left undeveloped and deserted. Setbacks, ratios of land occupation, and the vast expanses of road surfaces are also harmful due to sun exposure and associated heat gain (Ben-Hamouche, 2013).

Landscape architecture is new to the region, both academically and professionally. Its decontextualized introduction by modern Western practitioners resulted in aesthetic and physical aspects, rather than ecological performance, being the primary focus of the nascent profession in the UAE during its early stages (Makhzoumi, 2002; Moosavi, Makhzoumi, & Grose, 2016). The resulting ‘beautification’, also referred to as ‘para-scaping’, aspires to the aesthetics of paradise as described in the Holy Quran, and is often meant to attract global acclaim. Beautification efforts, combined with limited horticultural knowledge about local plant species, led to the development of de-contextualized landscapes that need constant maintenance to survive yet provide limited eco-system services (Moosavi et al., 2016).

However, as technology advances and the landscape architecture profession in the region evolves, there is potential for landscapes to be designed for positive net carbon storage while also creating comfortable outdoor spaces that enhance the livability of neighborhoods. The benefits of urban trees and urban forests are well documented. In addition to providing thermal comfort through shading and evaporative cooling, trees provide protection from soil erosion, absorb noise, and serve a range of aesthetic and psychological benefits when located in urban areas (See Nowak & Dwyer, 2007; Roy, Byrne, & Pickering, 2012; Tyrväinen, Pauleit, Seeland, & de Vries, 2005). Even though the concept of planting trees in the desert seems counter-intuitive, research conducted for various arid regions globally has shown substantial benefits (even as weighed against costs and externalities) of trees as carbon farms (Becker, Wulfmeyer, Berger, Gebel, & Münch, 2013; Ornstein, Aleinov, & Rind, 2009; Tal & Gurion, 2009). These benefits, however, remain conditional upon a variety of factors that include the appropriateness of tree species, irrigation methods, water quality, and sustainable planting practices.

This paper outlines the potential for the planting of urban trees for net positive carbon storage under various water-energy regimes to produce near-zero or positive net carbon villa neighborhoods in Abu Dhabi. The following section outlines the modeling approach, including the 4 water-energy regimes adopted for this paper, the calculation of the operational carbon footprints for a variety of selected tree species under the 4 regimes, and a neighborhood scale analysis. The third section presents the results of the study, including species-specific results for each water-energy regime, as well as neighborhood scale results. The fourth section describes the limitations and areas for further research, followed by a discussion and conclusion on the larger implications of this study.

## **2. Methods**

## _2.1. Projective design_

For this study, we estimated the water demand and resulting net carbon emissions for growing 15 species of landscape trees native to or appropriate for use in Abu Dhabi and other arid regions using existing published allometric and water demand databases (Strutt, Wilson, Shorney-Darby, Shaw, & Byers, 2008). These results were then used to test four neighborhood scale planting scenarios and household energy efficiency standards to estimate neighborhood scale net storage

## _2.2. Proxy data_

At the time of writing and per a literature search by the authors, only seagrass beds, mangroves, and date palms have been studied in Abu Dhabi for carbon storage or allometry (Issa, Dahy, Ksiksi, & Sleous et al., n.d; Schile et al., 2017). Field measurements to establish or validate tree allometry, carbon storage, and water needs in situ are not currently feasible for many species identified in this study due to extremely low or non-existent sample sizes found by the author during site visits to neighborhoods (e.g. _Eucalyptus microtheca_ , _Pinus brutia_ ). Access to trees on private property for measurement also requires breaching customary standards of privacy and is better done by Emirati researchers at local universities or government agencies. Proxy data for watering needs, tree growth, and carbon storage from similar climatic regions in the United States was used instead to provide a tractable preliminary and projective investigation of current and future potential for carbon storage in the GCC region.

## _2.3. Water demand + carbon storage_

The water needs and net carbon storage rates were calculated for 4 water-energy regimes and for trees at 20 years of age as most species have reached a mature height of 6 m (∼19.6 feet) or higher by this age

(Bassuk, Curtis, Marranca, & Neal, 2003) and have more accurate allometric equations (Foroughbakhch, Háuad, Cespedes, Ponce, & González, 2001; Peper, McPherson, & Mori, 2001). Additionally, 20 years provides a reasonable and somewhat conservative figure to compare carbon storage across species at maturity (e.g. a typical _Eucalyptus microthea_ tree sequesters 38.5 C at age 20 compared to an average of 43.9 kg C/yr from age 20 to 50 years (Tree Carbon Calculator (CTCC), 2008)). Lastly, while normalization to a species’ entire lifetime has been used in storage studies, doing so requires older established landscapes to accurately assess (Nowak, Stevens, Sisinni, & Luley, 2002). Most existing vegetation in Abu Dhabi is less than 50 years old, so lifespans are not known for most species.

Carbon storage rates were estimated using the CUFR Tree Carbon Calculator (CTCC) which provides data on total and yearly carbon storage for a typical tree, categorized by location in specific U.S. climate zones. Only species from the ‘desert’ or ‘tropical’ climate zone were used as the closest alternative for Abu Dhabi’s climate. Tree carbon calculations in the CTCC are based on growth curves developed from samples of 650–1000 street trees representing approximately 20–30 predominant species in each of the climatic regional reference cities. To estimate carbon storage of species not present in the database, the CTCC manual recommends using species from the same climate zone with the most similar growth rate and mature size.

## _2.4. Four water-energy regimes_

Four currently possible water-energy regimes (water production, pumping, and energy source) (Table 1) for Abu Dhabi were used to calculate the carbon emissions and the subsequent net capacity for supporting each of the 15 tree species. For each regime, 100 percent implementation of the given water and energy technologies was assumed. This was done to understand the relative net storage potential of each tree-water-energy regime independently. The 4 regimes are described below.

## Reverse Osmosis Desalination using Grid Electricity (RO-G)

Currently, the remaining 7 percent of desalinated water supply is produced through the reverse osmosis desalination (RO) process that is powered by grid electricity (that is produced by the MSF co-generation plants). This technology, where semipermeable membranes are used to separate unwanted molecules and ions from the water solvent, is becoming increasingly popular in the region. In the UAE, seven new RO plants (and no new MSF plants) have been planned for construction (Dawoud, 2012). Existing RO plants require between 2.5 and 4 kWh/m[3] of desalinated water, which we have used as low and high values for our calculations (Amy et al., 2017; Plappally & Lienhard, 2012).

## Reverse Osmosis Desalination using Solar Photovoltaic Electricity (RO-S)

In this regime, reverse osmosis desalination is powered by lowcarbon, rooftop and ground mounted solar photovoltaic (PV) panels. Solar PV technology has advanced rapidly in the last decade, with major reductions in price. Recent bids for utility-scale solar projects have been as low as USD 0.024 kWh, making solar competitive with the current USD0.08/kWh delivered cost of MSF grid energy (Fehrenbacher, 2016; Mokri, Aal Ali, & Emziane, 2013). The low cost of solar has led to increasingly aggressive transitional strategies in the region. Dubai, for example, has targeted 75% solar energy by 2050 and now mandates solar-PV panels on all new buildings (Richardson, 2015).

## Recycled Water using Solar Photovoltaic Electricity (RE-S)

This regime presents a future modelled scenario where the existing recycled wastewater system is transitioned to being powered by solar energy and all tree vegetation is irrigated by the recycled wastewater. In such a scenario, the amount of water available for landscaping is constrained to the amount of water used for indoor purposes and captured in the sewer system.

## _2.6. Tree species selection_

A list of 15 species was created by cross referencing species between the Center for Urban Forest Research (CUFR) database, which provides tree carbon storage data, the Water Use Classification of Landscape Species (WUCOLS) database (Costello & Jones, 2014), which provides empirically-validated water demand data relative to a region’s reference evapotranspiration (ETo), and Abu Dhabi’s Public Realm Design Manual (ADPRDM), which recommends native and regionally appropriate species for parks, streetscapes, and other public areas in the emirate. Species were primarily selected based on a combination of regional appropriateness for neighborhood landscaping as outlined by the ADPRDM and carbon storage potential as calculated by CUFR. All species selected are desert or tropical species and viable for the arid, desert context of Abu Dhabi. All 15 species are present in the CUFR database, allowing direct calculation of carbon storage by age or DBH. Nine species are present in the ADPRDM and considered native, while the remaining 6 can be considered non-native, but appropriate for the climate. When species were not present in the WUCOLS database, the ADPRDM’s water classification was used to estimate water demands. All species in the list have empirically validated data for carbon storage and water demands based on tree characteristics (age, DBH) and climate.

To spatialize carbon storage results and make net storage calculations at the neighborhood scale possible, net storage per species was linked to averaged canopy area by age or DBH. Readers should note that differences in tree maintenance, pruning, local grouping and shading generate will generate a high variance in canopy size between individual trees. Nevertheless, for each species in the final list, canopy diameter was calculated from tree height, diameter at breast height (DBH), or age using allometric equations. For 6 of the 15 species, ( _Cupaniopsis anacardioides_ , _Delonix regia_ , _Eucalyptus microtheca_ , _Melaleuca quinquenervia_ , _Phoenix Dactylifera_ , _Pinus brutia_ ) genus and species matches to allometric equations were found in literature (Arzai & Aliyu, 2010; Avsar, 2004; McPherson, van Doorn, & Peper, 2016; O’Brien, Hubbell, Spiro, Condit, & Foster, 1995; Peper et al., 2001). These will produce the most reliable results and have standard error of estimates (S) provided in Appendices A and B. For the remaining 9 species, growth equations were assigned using best-practices and based on similar genus when possible, and when not possible, based on morphological features such as stem, branch, leaf, height, and canopy shape and size. These species are marked by a * in Appendices A and B. Carbon storage rates were calculated using empirical data within the CUFR model. ## _2.7. Tree operational carbon footprint (Tcfp) and tree carbon storage (Tseq)_

Firstly, the volume of water (in cubic meters per year) required to irrigate a typical 20-year-old tree for each species was calculated. The reference evapotranspiration rate (ETo) of Abu Dhabi was determined to be 2437 mm/yr for the climate station at the Abu Dhabi International Airport (24.43° N, 54.65° E, 27 m.) using the United Nations’ Food and Agriculture Organization’s (FAO’s) ClimWat 2.0 and ETo 3.2 software (CLIMWAT, 2000; ETo Calculator, 2009). The ETo rate equals the water required for a reference grass crop that is well watered throughout the year and generally provides an upper limit on water demand for any tree, shrub, or crop per unit of land area cover (Allen, Pereira, Raes, & Smith, 1998). The watering needs for other plant species (Kc) are captured as a percentage of ETo, typically from 10 to 90%. Additional watering adjustments can be made for non-standard conditions such as drought irrigation or wind factors. To estimate watering needs of tree species (Kc) planted in Abu Dhabi we used the WUCOLS database (Appendix C). The WUCOLS database Kc values are derived from field observations by horticulturalists specializing in plants within each of the 18 California Irrigation and Management Information Systems Climatic Zones, including California’s high and low desert regions. Combined drip irrigation efficiency and distribution losses of 15 percent were estimated from empirical studies (Columbia University, 2010; Evans, 2010).

Tree species and age were used in conjunction with allometric equations (Appendices A and B) from the literature to model the canopy diameter. Canopy area per tree, derived from canopy diameter, was then used in conjunction with the species watering coefficient from the WUCOLS database, and the ETo value, to estimate water needs for individual species. The Tcfp for each species was then calculated for each of the 4 water-energy regimes by multiplying low and high-water production energy demand and carbon emission factors by the volume of water needed for a given species for a year. The tree carbon storage potential (Tseq) for each species at 20 years of age was determined using the CUFR model (Appendix D). Lastly, net carbon storage (Tnc) for each species and water-energy regime was calculated by subtracting Tseq from Tcfp. Long-term carbon storage potential is shown in Fig. 3 below.

## _2.8. Neighborhood scale studies_

A neighborhood scale analysis was conducted to spatialize the relationship between operational carbon emissions from household energy use and the required number and area of trees required to offset those emissions under various scenarios of electricity carbon factor, house energy efficiency, house size, planting area, and species combinations. This aided in understanding the potential for both older existing and newly constructed neighborhoods to achieve near-zero operational carbon balances. It also allowed an understanding of the sufficiency of existing building standards for lowering carbon footprints and framed the discussion on open-space use in neighborhood design.

For this analysis, the Old Al Bahya neighborhood was selected because: a) it is fully built-out, b) existing vegetation is mature providing accurate baseline, c) has high ratio of plantable open space, and d) the neighborhood design adheres to principles of the traditional _fareej_ layout. Built in the 1990s, the neighborhood spans approximately 440,000 m[2] with an unpaved and unbuilt plantable area of

approximately 175,000 m[2] (40%) as calculated by the authors using a combination of GIS data for building footprints and roadways. Satellite imagery was used to verify GIS data and manually draw tree canopy and driveways not included in GIS data. We estimate 5% or less error in area calculations. There are roughly 230 houses with an estimated population of 1610 assuming average household size of 7 members (“Department of Urban Planning and Municipalities – Community Facility Planning Standards, 2007).

Emissions from household operational energy (cooling, lighting, and equipment) is estimated using normalized energy use intensity (EUI) data (kWh/m[2] /yr) multiplied by house size and carbon emissions factor per energy source. An empirical study of existing, non-Estidama conforming Emirati houses (baseline) showed EUI’s of 349 kWh/m[2] /yr (Giusti & Almoosawi, 2017). Estidama is a rating system with a scale from 1 to 5 developed by the Abu Dhabi Urban Planning council to set guidelines for sustainable building practices (Abu Dhabi Urban Planning Council, 2010). The rating system and regulations went into effect in Fall 2010, whereby all new houses must be rated Pearl 1 or better. Newer, more efficient house designs, including Estidama conforming houses, tested or simulated in the region show significant energy savings and resulting EUI’s between 71 and 155 kWh/m[2] /yr (Alalouch, Saleh, & Al-Saadi, 2016; Birge & Berger, 2018; Masdar, 2017). Birge and Berger (2018) was used to set EUI’s based on house size and construction standard. Electricity from Abu Dhabi’s grid has a carbon factor of 0.47 kg CO2/kWh while energy from currently manufactured CdTe photovoltaic panels have a carbon factor of 0.011 kg CO2/kWh. (First First Solar, 2018; (Mariska) de Wild-Scholten, 2013; The Environment Agency, 2012). CdTe panels offer superior hightemperature performance relative to crystalline silicone panels and were chosen for this reason (Rix, Steyl, Rudman, Terblanche, & van Niekerk, 2015)

## _2.9. Neighborhood vegetation planting scenarios_

Four planting scenarios were developed for the neighborhood analysis process (Fig. 2). The first modeled the existing conditions (using satellite imagery), and the remaining 3 modeled increasing levels of vegetation density measured using canopy coverage (canopy area projected orthogonally onto the ground plane). A low and high net storage value per m[2] of canopy was calculated assuming RO-Desal and using canopy area results from Appendix C and mean net storage results from Appendix D. The low value equals 0.27 kg C/m[2] /yr, the average net storage rate from nine species selected from the ADPRDM database. The high value equals 0.55 kg C/m[2] /yr, the average net storage from the five highest sequestering species in the list.

## **3. Results**

## _3.1. Results from individual water-energy regimes_

This section contains results of the study including: species-specific results for each of the 4 water-energy regimes, a comparative analysis of these species-specific results, and results of the neighborhood scale analysis (see Table 2).

_MSF: Multi-Stage Flash (baseline):_ Under this regime, all 15 tree species were found to have net negative carbon storage. The range of net storage is large, from a low of −49.09 kg C/tree/yr for the _Parkinsonia aculeate_ (Jerusalem Thorn) to a high of −283.36 kg C/tree/ yr for the _Eucalyptus microtheca_ (Coolibah Tree). Selecting water conserving trees matters the most if MSF water is used for irrigation.

_RO-G: RO Desalination and Grid Electricity:_ The average net storage of all 15 species in the study under RO-G (−9.27 kg C/tree/yr) was found to be 16 times less than MSF regime (−147.80 kg C/tree/yr).

Depending on RO plant type and energy efficiency, 1– 5 species of the 15 could achieve net positive storage, but not at a significant enough rate to be meaningfully used for carbon offsetting.

_RO-S: RO Desalination and Solar PV:_ All tree species had positive mean storage values with a low of 1.50 kg C/tree/yr for _Phoenix dactylifera_ (Date Palm) and high of 38.18 kg C/tree/yr for _Eucalyptus microtheca_ (Coolibah tree). The average net storage for all 15 species was 15.00 kg C/tree/yr, for the 9 native species was 10.36 kg C/tree/yr, and for the 5 highest sequestering species was 26.72 kg C/tree/yr. The factor of 3 difference in storage between highest sequestering species and native species may be significant enough to result in a strong preference for highest sequestering species species in the future which would alter the landscape aesthetics of Emirati neighborhoods.

_RE-S: Recycled Water and Solar PV:_ This regime produces the highest net positive carbon storage potential due to the lower energy needs of water recycling relative to desalination. However, the use of recycled water has a number of limitations, including: 1) Its net carbon benefit is relatively minor compared to desalination (on average, approximately 5 percent); 2) Its supply is limited by prior potable water usage which causes a conflict between indoor water conservation and increasing landscape water demands; and 3) Its use for landscaping that humans may come in contact with raises health concerns (Bazza, 2003; Dawoud, Sallam, & Abdelfattah, 2012). A better use for recycled water would likely be in farms which allow for controlled and isolated growing conditions which are currently dependent on rapidly-depleting ground water (Al-Katheeri, 2008).

## _3.2. Comparative water-energy results_

The results show that larger, faster growing trees _(Eucalyptus microtheca_ , _Ulmus parvifolia_ , _Acacia salicina, Morus alba_ ) require more water and as a result provide the most extreme results. When carbon emissions per unit of water is highly positive (MSF regime), watering large, fast growing trees results in high emissions. However, when emissions per unit of water is low, as in the case of RO-S and RE-S, large, fast growing trees store 5–20 times more carbon than is emitted for their watering (Appendix D). In short, the worst performing trees in terms of carbon emissions under the current MSF regime are also the best performing trees in terms of carbon emissions under the RO-S or RE-S regimes (e.g. _Eucalyptus microtheca_ : −283 kg C/tree/yr MSF; +40 kg C/tree/yr RO-S).

## _3.3. Canopy diameter_

Due to morphological differences between tree species, carbon storage rates will vary by canopy area as well as by height and age (more typical metrics). This is an important consideration when planting trees for carbon storage as trees with higher storage rates per canopy area can provide more efficient use of limited land area, especially in urban and suburban areas. Fig. 3 shows the relationship between canopy diameter and carbon storage. As an example, at full maturity, when tree height has stabilized (at least according to the models), a specimen of _Melaleuca quinquenervia_ will have stored roughly 650 kg C per m[2] of canopy area, whereas _Eucalyptus microtheca_ will have stored roughly 250 kg C per m[2] of canopy (see Fig. 3 below). Therefore, all else being equal, and allowing equal spacing between canopy boundaries, planting with _Eucalyptus microtheca_ would require 160% more land to store the same amount of carbon over a landscape’s lifetime. Potential errors in the results for trees using proxy data should be taken into account as should the growth rate of trees.

## **4. Discussion**

The results from this study show that current and future neighborhood scale landscaping can sequester and offset a significant amount of emissions from villa energy use (cooling, lighting, equipment) when water is produced from RO desalination and when desalination and residential energy is sourced from solar-PV. Under this RO-S waterenergy regime, assuming 50–80% tree canopy coverage in a neighborhood, the final percent of carbon emissions sequestrated by trees can vary considerably from a low of 15% to a high of 800%, and depends on multiple factors including house construction standards, house size, planting area, and species selection. This highlights the sensitivity of carbon balances to both technology and design factors and indicates that a wide range of neighborhood typologies can achieve near-zero carbon operations in the near future.

While further research and system parameterization is required to include additional operational and embodied emissions, it is also plausible that by 2050, if not earlier, suburban neighborhood

typologies in Abu Dhabi and other arid regions could be designed, built, and planted to be carbon neutral for all major emission sources arising from water, transportation, and housing operations. If true, the generally held assumption within the urban planning discipline that lowdensity residential neighborhoods should not be built due in part to their higher building and transportation energy use would be contested and partially disproved (Norman, MacLean, & Kennedy, 2006; Rickwood, 2009). This is a significant finding given the current and likely continued preference for single-family homes both in Abu Dhabi and throughout the world (A planet of suburbs, 2018; Berger & Kotkin, 2017). Not only can low-density neighborhoods in Abu Dhabi become carbon neutral but the additional social and environmental benefits of trees, along with the ability to integrate carbon storage into neighborhoods (thus limiting additional land-uses outside the neighborhood) may ultimately prove to be an equal or better option towards carbon neutrality than building denser housing with secondary forestation in planned areas outside of a city.

To achieve carbon neutral neighborhoods, however, will require overcoming the following potentially limiting factors: first, the inclusion and use of new (non-native) arid tree species, and second, the desalination of additional water to support proposed vegetation. The potential negative ramifications of introducing non-native species of flora and fauna into new regions is well documented (Pimentel, Zuniga, & Morrison, 2005). Concerns such as high-water demand, rapid propagation, and ecosystem disruption from non-native species might present valid challenges to the results of this study. In Abu Dhabi, in

2012 non-native species accounted for 65% of vegetation in ornamental landscape projects, which require more water and are not drought-resistant. However, the non-native species selected for this study are all desert or arid species and similar to native species in terms of water demand. While ecosystem impacts need further research, the existing arid landscape of Abu Dhabi is a hostile environment for plant growth resulting in the need for intentional planting, and constant active irrigation and maintenance. Therefore, unintentional propagation of trees is not a concern.

Assuming non-native, high-carbon fixing species can be planted in the region with no adverse ecological impacts, watering remains a potential hurdle. At 80% canopy coverage (140,000 m[2] ) and using highest sequestering species, the neighborhood in this study would require 182,000 m[3] /yr of water for irrigation. Upon completion in 2021, the Al Taweelah RO plant extension (45 km North of Abu Dhabi) will produce 328,500,000 m[3] /yr from two separate plants (Asaba, 2018). The Al Taweelah plant could, therefore, support landscape watering for 1800 neighborhoods of the size and open-space ratio used in this study. This would equal 790 km[2] of neighborhood fabric. For comparison, the white area outlined in Fig. 1, denoting the current lowrise neighborhood extents in Abu Dhabi, equals 250 km[2] . The additional water production for neighborhood scale afforestation for all current and likely future suburbs in Abu Dhabi is possible with the addition of a single new desalination plant.

The prospect of large areas of artificially-watered landscapes in Abu Dhabi hypothesized in this study raises a final question about city building in arid regions. Should synthetic potable water be added to the list of other artificial metabolic flows already needed to support both arid and temperate cities alike including artificial lighting, heating, cooling, refrigeration, and highly mechanized transportation and agricultural production? Or, is artificial (desalinated) water unique in its externalities and costs such that coastal arid regions should seek to limit the use of desalinated water for landscaping into the future? The answer to this question has broad implications not only for the future of established cities such as Abu Dhabi, but for the establishment of new urban and suburban areas in fast-growing arid regions globally.

## _4.1. Limitations and future research_

Before discussing the broader implications of our results, several limitations and future areas of research should be pointed out which would improve the accuracy of our findings and increase the scope of parameters considered. These future studies and improvements include:

1. Empirical studies from adequate sample sizes in the region to improve the accuracy of a) passive house EUI’s, b) tree Kc factors (water demand), c) tree allometry, and d) tree carbon storage rates. This will lower margins of errors induced from proxy studies, strengthen the overall conclusions of this initial study, and aid in developing more specific neighborhood land-use ratios and housing typologies.

2. Some of the conclusions of this study depend on the proposed planting of highest sequestering species which are not currently present in adequate numbers the region. Controlled planting and measuring of water demands, carbon storage, and allometry over 20 years or more would establish the costs, maintenance needs, and critical performance parameters of these species in the Abu Dhabi context.

3. Neighborhood carbon balance studies that include other neighborhood emission sources including tree planting and maintenance, automobile use, and embodied emissions from road construction, house construction, and vehicle and battery manufacturing would

   - significantly increase the scope, though not necessarily the magnitude, of emission sources considered.

4. Empirical cost-benefit analysis of additional social, cultural, and environmental benefits provided by neighborhood vegetation in the Abu Dhabi context. These services, which been established in Western context, include but are not limited to increased privacy, increased walkability, noise reduction, improved air quality, microclimatic cooling, building energy savings, increase property values, and increased outdoor space use (McPherson, Simpson, Xiao, & Wu, 2011; Shackleton, Chinyimba, Hebinck, Shackleton, & Kaoma, 2015; Song, Richards, Edwards, & Tan, 2017).

5. The near term plausibility of the RO-S regime should be studied further including: 1) a detailed scalability assessment of RO desalination to meet watering demands of future potential urban forests (see discussion for high-level assessment); 2) the cost of desalinated water as a share of total costs of tree planting and maintenance and relative to carbon credits or other offsetting ecosystem services; 3) mitigation of saline discharge and harmful impacts on the environment; and 4) analysis of solar-PV grid integration and energy storage needs for optimal operation.

6. The optimal location of solar-PV panel deployment must be evaluated in light of the potential for significant shading from mature trees. Panels may be better situated on the outskirts of neighborhoods or in larger community or utility scale projects supported by neighborhood development. The problem of whether solar supply or carbon storage should be prioritized in neighborhoods is an important next step. Given the secondary benefits of vegetation (microclimate, aesthetics, shading, air-quality), and limited secondary benefits of solar (off-grid operation), it seems self-evident that vegetation should generally be given first priority.

## **5. Conclusion**

Recent improvements to solar photovoltaic and reverse-osmosis desalination technology has lowered the carbon emissions for water production from 12.79 kg CO2/m[3] (current MSF) to 0.032–0.132 kg CO2/m[3] . This allows trees planted in hot, desert climates to be watered with treated ocean water while achieving net storage rates of between 1.7 and 38.2 kg C/tree/yr depending on species depending on species. When planted in existing neighborhood open spaces, we find that storage rates are meaningful relative to household emission rates (15–800% depending on parameters) when household energy comes from solar-PV (or similar carbon factor). Additional benefits from urban and suburban forests including improved privacy, microclimate cooling, air pollution reduction, and increased walkability, would enhance overall livability in arid regions. The impact on year-round outdoor human comfort to allow longer seasonal outdoor space use could be wide ranging. Assuming secondary factors associated with ROS desalination can be overcome (e.g. high-saline discharge, renewable energy storage, costs) we contend the future role of landscaped open spaces using broad shade tree planting palettes, currently seen as environmentally unsustainable, should be rethought in arid and desert regions based on the numerous benefits they can provide.

**Alan M. Berger** is the Norman B. and Muriel Leventhal Professor of Advanced Urbanism at Massachusetts Institute of Technology, where he co-directs LCAU and P-REX lab. His most recent book is Infinite Suburbia (with Joel Kotkin, Celina Balderas Guzman), a global perspective on suburban expansion. In addition to his award-winning books Drosscape: Wasting Land in Urban America, and Reclaiming the American West, his other books include Designing the Reclaimed Landscape, and The Infrastructural Monument and Scaling Infrastructure (with Alexander D'Hooghe). Prior to MIT, Berger was Associate Professor of Landscape Architecture at Harvard-GSD. He is a Prince Charitable Trusts Fellow of The American Academy in Rome.
